scenarios.title: Investing money
scenarios.when: Normal conditions. Over several weeks, paused while you compare options.
scenarios.text: Imagine you are deciding whether to spend a sum that matters to you on something that should help you earn more: equipment, a course, a tool or stock. You have a few weeks, and the decision pauses while you compare options.

opts: I build the case: what it costs, what it should bring back and how long until it pays for itself.
With a sense of whether it is the right next step for me.

q.ask: When you come back to it after comparing the options, what do you turn to?
opts: How it would feel to have it, and what the people around me would think.
Whether the prices and the payback numbers support what I first felt.
The numbers add up and it makes sense.
It feels right for where I am going.

scenarios.title: Investing money
scenarios.when: Under stress: money at risk and time pressure. Decided today.
scenarios.text: Imagine the same thing is offered at 40% off, today only. Taking it would use most of what you have put aside for the next two months.

opts: I calculate what the saving is worth against two months with nothing in reserve.
I read the offer: whether it feels like a real win or a trap, and what I feel about the seller.

q.ask: What do you check before deciding?
opts: How it would feel to run two months with no cushion, and what the people close to me would say.
Whether the saving and the money I have really support the move.
What the saving and my money add up to.
Whether the deal is good for me and feels right.

scenarios.title: Pricing
scenarios.text: Imagine you are putting a price on something you are offering: your work, a product, a service or something you are selling. You know what it costs you, what others charge and what two or three interested people have said. You have a week.

opts: With what it costs me, what I need to keep and what others charge.
With what it is worth to the buyer and what price feels right to me.

q.ask: During the week, what do you keep coming back to?
opts: How buyers will react to the price.
Whether the figures back up the price I have in mind.
The figures work: it should be profitable.
It feels right: it is the best offering out there.

scenarios.title: Pricing
scenarios.when: Under stress: conflict and money. Decided today.
scenarios.text: Imagine the buyer who matters most to you says they will walk away unless you drop the price by 15%. They want an answer by the end of the day.

opts: I work out what 15% does to what I keep, and what losing them would cost.
I get a sense of whether they mean it, and what I want this relationship to be.

q.ask: What do you check before you answer?
opts: How the relationship would feel at the lower price.
Whether I can actually carry the cut.

q.ask: What settles your answer, whichever way it goes?
opts: What the figures say: can I afford it?
What feels right: is it worth it?

scenarios.title: Choosing who to work with
scenarios.when: Normal conditions. Over a month, in several conversations.
scenarios.text: Imagine someone you have known for two years proposes doing something together: a venture, a project or a joint piece of work. You have a month and several conversations before you answer.

opts: I define what each of us would bring, how the roles and the money would work and what could go wrong.
I notice how the idea and the person feel: the energy of the conversations and whether I can see the story working.

q.ask: Between the conversations, what do you turn to?
opts: How working with them every day would feel, and how the people around us would react.
Whether the facts support my first response: what they have done before, the market and the numbers.
The structure adds up: roles, money and risks are clear and I can defend each one.
It feels right: the partnership and the vision sit well with me.

scenarios.title: Disagreeing with the person you build with
scenarios.when: Under stress: conflict. Decided in minutes.
scenarios.text: Imagine a meeting with the person you are building something with: a partner, a collaborator or someone whose backing you need. They argue strongly for a direction you disagree with. Others are watching. The decision has to be made before you leave the room.

opts: I go to the facts: which option the numbers and constraints support, and where their argument has gaps.
I go to my sense of the room and the direction: what feels right for the work, the relationship and everyone.

q.ask: Before you speak, what do you check?
opts: How each option would feel to them and to the others, and what it would do to trust.
Whether the evidence actually supports the option I am drawn to.

q.ask: What settles the decision for you?
opts: The data that adds up, and I explain the reasoning.
The story that feels right, and I explain why it matters.

scenarios.title: Launching
scenarios.when: Normal conditions. Over a month, in and out of other work.
scenarios.text: Imagine you are deciding when to put something out: an offer, a website, a product or an announcement. The decision runs over a month, alongside everything else.

opts: I set the criteria: what must be ready, tested and measurable before it goes out.
I can tell when it and its story will be ready, and what moment the people I want to reach are in.

q.ask: As the month goes on, what do you keep checking?
opts: How it would land with the people I want to reach at each possible date.
Whether the checklist and the numbers support the date I have in mind.
The criteria are met and the plan adds up.
It looks ready and the story is right.

scenarios.title: Launching
scenarios.when: Under stress: time pressure. Decided in minutes.
scenarios.text: Imagine it is the day. An hour before it goes live, something breaks: a payment page, a link, a file. People have been told the time. Go ahead or delay, needs to be decided in the next few minutes.

opts: I size the problem: how many people it affects, what a fix takes and what a delay costs.
I read the moment: what going ahead or delaying would feel like for the people waiting and for me.
How the people waiting would feel if we delayed, or went ahead as it is.
Whether the fix time and the numbers actually support delaying or going ahead.

q.ask: What settles it, go or delay?
opts: The option that adds up, even if people get upset.
The option that feels right, even if it costs us.

scenarios.title: A personal decision
scenarios.text: Imagine you are deciding whether to move to another place. It would help what you are building and change daily life for you and the people close to you. The decision runs over two months.

opts: I list the facts: costs, travel, what I gain and what we lose.
I notice how the move feels: whether I can see myself there and whether the next few years’ story fits.

q.ask: Over the two months, what do you keep turning to?
opts: How the people close to me feel about it, and how daily life would feel there.
Whether the costs and the case for moving support what I first felt.
The numbers and the practicalities add up.
It just feels right and is the best thing for me.

scenarios.title: A personal decision
scenarios.when: Under stress: money and a relationship. Decided in seconds.
scenarios.text: Imagine your closest friend rings tonight to ask to borrow money for something really important to them. The only money you have is what you had set aside for what you are building. They need an answer now.

opts: I work out what I can afford, what that money was for and when I would get it back.
I focus on the relationship and what feels right between us.

q.ask: Before you answer, what do you check?
opts: How saying yes or no would feel for both of us.
Whether the money actually works, whatever I feel.
What adds up and makes sense.
What feels like the right thing to do.

scenarios.title: Accepting an offer
scenarios.text: Imagine an offer that would change your plans: a contract, a customer, a role or a collaboration. You have three weeks to answer.

opts: I model what it takes: time, money, what I would have to give up and the risk if it falls through.
I notice whether this is the opening I have been waiting for and whether it feels like my next chapter.

q.ask: Over the three weeks, what do you turn to?
opts: The impact on the people around me: how they would feel about the change, and how I would feel living it.
Whether the time and the money numbers support the risk and sacrifice.
The case adds up: it is worth it.
It feels right: it would benefit me.

scenarios.title: Accepting an offer
scenarios.when: Under stress: time pressure and money. Decided within 24 hours.
scenarios.text: Imagine the same offer, but they need a yes within 24 hours, and saying yes would stretch your time and your money.

opts: I run what the stretch costs in time and money and whether I can cover it.
I read the opportunity: whether it feels right to stretch for this now.

q.ask: Before you answer, what do you check?
opts: How the people around me would feel about the stretch, and how they would feel about a no.
Whether the money and the time actually work.
What adds up: it is profitable.
What feels right: it is beneficial.

scenarios.title: Ending an arrangement
scenarios.text: Imagine ending something that no longer works for you: a supplier, a client, a subscription or a commitment. You are deciding over a month.

opts: I lay out the numbers: what it costs me, what it gives me and what I could do instead.
I notice how it feels now, how it affects everyone, and what ending it would mean for my story and everyone involved.

q.ask: Over the month, what do you keep coming back to?
opts: How the other side and the people around me would feel about ending it.
Whether the figures and the alternatives support ending it.
The numbers add up.
What is best for everyone.

scenarios.title: Ending an arrangement
scenarios.when: Under stress: conflict. Decided in minutes.
scenarios.text: Imagine the other side says: drop your condition or we walk, now.

opts: I work out what dropping the condition costs and what losing them costs.
I feel the tension in the room straight away: whether they mean it, and what it does to the relationship.

q.ask: Before you answer, what do you check?
opts: How each answer would feel to them and to me.
Whether I can actually carry the change.
What the numbers support.
What’s the right thing to do.

part2.ask: You are building something new and the time you had has just been cut. What do you protect first?

o.MS: The plan: the order of the steps and which moves come first.
o.SB: The flow: the routine and the system that keep things running reliably.
o.IA: The accuracy: the data and the assumptions the work rests on.
o.UA: All three at once: the plan, the system and the data, adjusted together.
o.VO: The vision: the story and where this is going.
o.MP: The quality: what it looks and feels like, and the details that matter.
o.EE: The people: the momentum and the relationships around it.
o.UAl: All three at once: the vision, the quality and the people, kept in step.

part2.ctx: Fixing something that has gone wrong
part2.ask: Something you depend on has broken and everyone is looking to you. What do you protect first?

o.MS: The priorities: what has to happen first, second and third.
o.SB: The routine: keeping the parts that still work running reliably.
o.IA: The facts: finding out exactly what happened before anything changes.
o.UA: All three: the priorities, the routine and the facts, held together.
o.VO: The direction: making sure the setback does not change where we are going.
o.MP: The standard: not letting the fix lower the quality.
o.EE: The people: keeping everyone steady and together.
o.UAl: All three: the direction, the standard and the people, held together.

part2.ask: When you build something new, how does your work naturally run?

o.MS: In blocks: I set a few moves, run them for a stretch, then review and re-plan.
o.SB: Continuously: a weekly routine that keeps everything moving.
o.IA: In test cycles: run a test, check the results, decide the next one.
o.UA: All three: moves set in blocks, a weekly routine to run them, tests to prove them.
o.VO: In rounds: show a working version, get reactions, show the next.
o.MP: In polish cycles: refine until it is right, with a date to put it out.
o.EE: In conversations: talk with the people involved until we are aligned, then move.
o.UAl: All three: show it, refine it and bring people with it, in step.

part2.ctx: Fixing something that has gone wrong
part2.ask: When you are fixing something that has gone wrong, how do you work through it?

o.MS: I step back, re-order the priorities and set the next few moves.
o.SB: I put a routine on it: daily checks until it runs smoothly again.
o.IA: I run tests to find the cause before I change anything.
o.UA: All three: re-order the moves, put a routine on it and test the cause.
o.VO: I re-tell where we are going and test the next step towards it.
o.MP: I refine the part that failed until it is right, with a date to put it back out.
o.EE: I get the people involved together and agree the way through.
o.UAl: All three: re-tell the direction, refine what failed and bring people together.

part2.ask: A new idea keeps growing. How do you keep it in bounds?

o.MS: I tie everything to the moves I chose and cut what does not serve them.
o.SB: I standardise: once something works, it becomes the way we do it.
o.IA: Nothing is added until the analysis says it should be.
o.UA: All three: the chosen moves set the scope, standards hold it, analysis gates it.
o.VO: I let it explore while the pattern becomes clear, then settle it.
o.MP: I set the quality bar and cut everything that falls below it.
o.EE: I agree the scope with the people involved and hold us to it.
o.UAl: All three: explore, then set the bar, with everyone agreed.

part2.ctx: Fixing something that has gone wrong
part2.ask: In a crisis, requests pile up. How do you decide what gets done?

o.MS: By the plan: what moves the chosen priorities first.
o.SB: By the standard: what keeps the system running comes first.
o.IA: By the numbers: what the data says matters most.
o.UA: All three: the plan, the standard and the numbers together.
o.VO: By the direction: what keeps us on the course we are on.
o.MP: By the quality bar: what keeps the result right.
o.EE: By the people: what keeps everyone moving and together.
o.UAl: All three: the direction, the quality bar and the people together.

part2.ask: Pick the one thing you would create first on a new project.

o.MS: A roadmap or a map of the options.
o.SB: A checklist or a step-by-step procedure.
o.IA: A dashboard or a test plan.
o.UA: A one-page map that links the roadmap, the procedures and the tests.
o.VO: A story brief or a short video of what it will become.
o.MP: A quality bar: the standard the result must meet.
o.EE: A list of the people involved and what each has committed to.
o.UAl: A one-page vision that links the story, the standard and the people.

part2.ctx: Fixing something that has gone wrong
part2.ask: Something has gone wrong. What is the first thing you write down?

o.MS: A re-ordered plan: what comes first now.
o.SB: A procedure so it does not happen again.
o.IA: A record of what happened, with the numbers.
o.UA: One page with the new order, the procedure and the record together.
o.VO: The story of where we go from here.
o.MP: The standard the fix must meet.
o.EE: Who is doing what, and who needs to hear from me.
o.UAl: One page with the direction, the standard and the people together.

part2.ask: You are building something new and the pressure rises. What do you reach for first?

o.MS: I re-plan: step back and re-order the moves.
o.SB: I add process: more structure, more routine.
o.IA: I go deeper into the detail and the data.
o.UA: All three at once: re-plan, tighten the process and check the data.
o.VO: I re-tell the story and test the next step.
o.MP: I hold the quality bar, or raise it.
o.EE: I rally the people around it.
o.UAl: All three at once: re-tell the story, hold the quality and rally people.

part2.ctx: Fixing something that has gone wrong
part2.ask: When a project or task starts breaking down (delays, confusion, errors or misalignment), what is your first instinct?

o.MS: Zoom out, rethink the overall plan and re-order the steps so everything makes sense again.
o.SB: Tighten or redesign the workflow or routine so things run smoothly again.
o.IA: Analyse what is causing the issue, look at the data, and test logical fixes.
o.UA: Re-align everything at once: the plan, the process and the data behind it.
o.VO: Reframe the story or direction so it feels aligned again.
o.MP: Refine the quality: adjust the detail until it feels right.
o.EE: Reset the energy: clear the tension, reconnect people, restore alignment.
o.UAl: Re-harmonise everything at once: the idea, the quality and the people.

part3.text: Imagine a partner deciding when to launch. In the meeting she says: “Before we pick a date I want the list: what is built, what is tested and what we will measure. Once that is done, let’s hear how customers are likely to react.” She sets the date when every item on the list is ticked.

She decides differently from me.
I cannot tell from this.

part3.ctx: Launching, with a partner who thinks differently from you

architect.ask: What are they really asking for, put in a way you could act on?

opts.t: A target for how many people are signed up or talking about it before the open date, and one moment in the launch built to be talked about.
More marketing: add a promotion to the plan.
They have not thought about the operations; park it until the plan is ready.

alchemist.text: Imagine your partner, who thinks differently from you, says: “Before we commit to the date, I need to know how many people we can handle and at what point we would stop.”
alchemist.ask: What are they really asking for, put in a way you could act on?

opts.t: How many people we can look after well before the excitement outgrows us, and the point at which we would pause to protect that.
They want to slow it down; agree a later date.
They are nervous; reassure them and carry on.
A smaller launch.

part3.ctx: Two people who think alike but work differently
part3.text: Imagine two people who understand each other well in how they think, launching an offer together. One plans by working out which moves come first; the other makes things run reliably through routines.
part3.ask: Which order of steps works best?

opts.t: The planner sets the moves and the stop points; the builder turns them into a procedure and runs it; both review at the checkpoint.
The builder standardises the routine first; the planner fits the moves around it.
Both plan everything together in one document, then split the work.
The planner does both, because planning comes first.

part3.text: Imagine two entrepreneurs building a new offer together who think and operate differently: one goes with their sense of the right thing and the story; the other works it out from the facts and the plan.
part3.ask: Which order of steps works best?

opts.t: The one who goes with the story shows a working example; they decide together; the one who works from the facts writes the detailed plan and scales it.
The one who works from the facts writes the plan; the other tests it, then tells the story so people take it up.
Each builds their own version and they merge at the end.

Split it: each runs their own version for a week and compare.
Show them why your approach is the right one.
Let them have it to keep the peace.

architect.stmt: System first. Meaning emerges after the system makes sense.
blind: Slow to change direction on feeling signals
fail: A perfect model that never ships
Plans that break when conditions change
Misreading people whose signals are felt rather than stated
adapt: Order of content
Overview → Definitions → Constraints → Steps → Examples → Risks → Action

Everything the app gives you is written in this order: your workbooks, your report pages and every AI Architect answer. You see the whole picture and the limits first, then the steps, then what it looks like done and what could go wrong, and only then what to do. Nothing asks you to act before the system makes sense.
Tools you will be given
SOPs, checklists, dashboards, “what could go wrong” lists, decision trees, mind maps

Inside your workbooks: when an exercise asks you to plan, price, hire or launch, it gives you one of these to fill in: a step-by-step procedure, a checklist you tick off, a dashboard page of the numbers that matter, a “what could go wrong” list (you list how the plan could fail before you start), or a decision tree. A structure to fill in, not a blank page.
How AI Architect works with you
“What evidence would change your mind?” “Which assumption affects the result most?”

AI Architect challenges you the way you decide. When you bring it a decision, it works through your Decision Intelligence Loop with you: the data you have, how it feels and how people react, the new data that answers that, and the decision. It asks for the evidence and the assumption behind each step, and it tells you when your final decision rests on a feeling instead of the data.
Working rhythm
Weekly Plan → Do → Check → Act, or Scrum sprints of up to one month

Your action plans are cut into weekly or sprint-length cycles, each with a stop point (what tells you to stop) and a scale point (what tells you to do more). You know in advance when you review and what you review against.

alchemist.stmt: Feeling first. The story must feel right before the numbers line up.
fail: Frequent changes of direction that unsettle the team
adapt: Order of content
Story → Why it matters → Pattern → Principles → Guardrails → First moves → Measures

Everything the app gives you is written in this order: your workbooks, your report pages and every AI Alchemist answer. The story and why it matters come first, then the pattern, the few principles and guardrails to hold, then the first moves. The numbers come last, as measures of whether it worked. Nothing asks you to specify before you can see it.
Tools you will be given
Story briefs, hypothesis canvases, vision ladders, a working demo first

Inside your workbooks: when an exercise asks you to plan, price, hire or launch, it gives you a one-page story brief, a hypothesis canvas (what must be true for this to work), a vision ladder (from where you are to where you can see), or asks you to build a rough working example before any specification. Something to see and react to, not a form.
How AI Alchemist works with you
“What must be true?” “Which two constraints matter now?” “How will we know it worked?”

AI Alchemist challenges you the way you decide. When you bring it a decision, it works through your Decision Intelligence Loop with you: what feels right and the story, whether the numbers support it, what that does to the feeling, and the decision. It takes the vision as given, asks what must be true and which two constraints you will hold, and it tells you when your final decision rests on data you do not yet believe in.
Working rhythm
Sense → Test → Show, then blocks of time to write down what worked

Your action plans run as short sense-test-show cycles: notice the signal, try it, show it to someone. After each cycle the workbook books a block of time to write down what worked, so the breakthroughs become something your team can repeat.

mixed.stmt: A Dominant Decision Intelligence Loop cannot be identified yet.
causes: Strong conditioning (for example, years in a corporate role)
Constant firefighting to the point where it becomes conditioning or causes stress
Adapting to fit what past roles rewarded
risks: A jack of all trades, master of none
adapt: Find the loop
Workbooks, then retake E-DNA in about 4 weeks

Your first workbooks are built to find your Dominant Decision Intelligence Loop, not to teach a subject. Each exercise makes you decide something real and records which loop you began and finished with. After about 4 weeks you retake E-DNA and the result confirms your Core Type Decision Intelligence Loop Identity.
Two-track exercises
One Architect track and one Alchemist track for every exercise

Every exercise comes in two versions and you do both. Architect track: write down exactly what will be done and how success will be measured, then review progress at a set checkpoint. Alchemist track: describe the result you can see, then build a quick working example to show someone. Which one came easier, and which one you finished, is the evidence.
Guardrails
Fewer switches, a stated reason for every change of direction, a written record of each decision

While your loop is unconfirmed the workbooks add three guardrails to your plans: a limit on how many tasks you switch between in a week, a one-line reason you must write before changing direction, and a decision log. These are what stop the strategy drift and the loss of trust that Mixed people report.
How the AI mentors work with you
AI Architect and AI Alchemist, both, until your Dominant loop is confirmed

When you bring either mentor a decision, it works through the loop with you box by box (data, feeling, new data, decision) and records which loop you began and finished with, without warning you either way. For important decisions the app shows both mentors' answers side by side. Noticing which answer you act on is part of finding your loop.

D1_LEAN_WHY.alchemist: Most likely an Alchemist whose Dominant Decision Intelligence Loop is not yet strong, so you switch constantly.

MS.is: A Master Strategist is an Architect who executes by choosing the order of moves. Once a decision is made, you turn it into a sequence: which bets come first, what each one has to show before the next starts, and what you will say no to. You win by timing: the right bet at the right moment, not every bet at once.
exec: When time is cut
You protect the plan: the order of the steps and which moves come first. Quality, data and people are adjusted to fit the sequence, not the other way round.
Your rhythm
You work in blocks. You set a few moves, run them for a stretch, then stop, review and re-plan. Progress is measured at the review, not day to day.
Keeping scope in bounds
You tie everything to the moves you chose and cut what does not serve them. A good idea that is not on the sequence waits.
The first thing you create
A roadmap or a map of the options. Before a procedure, a dashboard or a brief, you want to see the moves laid out.
Under pressure
You step back and re-order the moves. When something breaks, your first act is to re-order the priorities and set the next few moves, then let the fix follow.
wrong: Over-planning
The roadmap gets more detailed while the market moves. The plan is checked against the plan, not against what customers did this week.
Missed opportunities
An opening that was not in the sequence is slow to register, because it does not fit the order you set.
Distance from the ground
You see the business through the plan. Signals that arrive as a feeling (a team that has gone quiet, a customer who hesitates) register late, because they do not arrive as numbers.
Strategy for show
A deck that describes the strategy replaces decisions that act on it. Roadmaps go rigid, feedback comes late, and the next review arrives before the lesson does.
improve: Shorter time from plan to learning
Every bet gets a midpoint check at week three or four, not only at the end of the block. If the early indicator is not moving, you decide then.
Regular demos
Show a working version of each bet to real customers inside the block. A demo is feedback you cannot plan around.
A stop or scale rule for every bet
Write, before the block starts, what would make you stop and what would make you do more. Then the review is a decision, not a debate.
games: The clock forces a move before the plan is complete.
Every move shapes what is available three moves later; two minutes a game.
The plan meets the dice and the other players; you re-plan every turn.
MS.exercise: Give one live bet a stop or scale rule and a week-4 check this week.
best: Several product lines or markets running at once
avoid: A crisis that needs a fix today: re-planning first delays it
A single product that needs daily operational grip rather than a sequence
Any plan you have not shown to a customer within the block
MS.ladder: From here, The Ultimate Architect is reached by adding the other two Architect ways of executing to your own. From the Internal Analyser: prove each bet with a test before you scale it. From the Systemised Builder: once a bet works, make it a routine so it runs without you. The Ultimate Architect holds all three: the sequence, the proof and the system.

IA.is: An Internal Analyser is an Architect who executes by being right. Once a decision is made, you turn it into a question that data can answer: what has to be true, how you would know, and what the numbers say. You win by precision: fewer wrong moves, because each one was tested first.
exec: When time is cut
You protect the accuracy: the data and the assumptions the work rests on. A plan built on a wrong number is not a plan.
Your rhythm
You work in test cycles. Run a test, check the results, decide the next one. The cycle is short and the reading is weekly.
Keeping scope in bounds
Nothing is added until the analysis says it should be. Scope grows by evidence, not by enthusiasm.
The first thing you create
A dashboard or a test plan. You want the measures in place before the work starts.
Under pressure
You go deeper into the detail and the data. When something breaks, you find out exactly what happened before anything changes.
wrong: Analysis that slows decisions
The next test is always one more test. The decision waits for a certainty the data cannot give.
Perfectionism
A model that is nearly right is treated as wrong. Time goes into the last decimal place, not the decision.
Undervaluing what is not written down
Experience that arrives as judgement rather than data is discounted, so the people who have it stop offering it.
Results other people do not buy into
The finding is right and the room does not move, because it was presented as numbers without the story.
improve: A shorter time to insight
Set the success criteria and the stopping rule before each test, so the test ends when the answer is good enough, not when it is perfect.
Findings as a simple story
Present each result as one sentence a non-analyst would repeat, with the numbers underneath it.
Two-week cycles
Keep each test to two weeks with a weekly reading. If it needs longer, it is two tests.
games: A fixed number of guesses: commit to the best answer you have.
Explain the word in 30 seconds; the first clue that works beats the perfect one.
IA.exercise: Write the stopping rule before your next analysis, and present the result as one sentence with the numbers underneath.
best: Experiments where the answer is worth the wait
avoid: Decisions that have to be made before the data exists
Presenting a finding without the one-sentence story
Running a test with no stopping rule
IA.ladder: From here, The Ultimate Architect is reached by adding the other two Architect ways of executing to your own. From the Master Strategist: put your tests in an order that serves a plan, so proof leads somewhere. From the Systemised Builder: turn a proven result into a routine that runs without you. The Ultimate Architect holds all three: the sequence, the proof and the system.

VO.is: A Visionary Oracle is an Alchemist who executes by seeing where things are going first. Once a decision is made, you turn it into a direction: the story of what this becomes, why now, and the first proof that it is real. You win by being early: the pattern you saw before others did.
exec: When time is cut
You protect the vision: the story and where this is going. Quality, people and plan are shaped to serve the direction.
Your rhythm
You work in rounds. Show a working version, get reactions, show the next. The reaction is the plan.
Keeping scope in bounds
You let an idea explore while the pattern becomes clear, then settle it. Scope is open early and closed late.
The first thing you create
A story brief or a short video of what it will become. Before a checklist or a dashboard, you want people to see it.
Under pressure
You re-tell the story and test the next step towards it. When something breaks, you make sure the setback does not change where you are going.
wrong: Constraints passed over
The direction is right and the budget, the team or the timeline was not in the picture. The story runs ahead of what can be built.
Weak handover
The people who execute get the vision but not the steps, so they fill the gap with guesses.
Frequent changes of direction
Each new pattern you see becomes a new direction. The team is unsettled, and the basics are missed while the story moves on.
A big vision with no structure
The story converts, and there is nothing underneath it to deliver what it promised.
improve: A working version every few weeks
Put the date of the next demo in the diary before you tell the next story. Show something that works to real customers every two to four weeks. The demo supplies the structure the story leaves out.
A must-be-true list for every idea
Before an idea becomes a direction, write the three things that must be true for it to work, and give yourself 30 days to prove them. If they are not true at day 30, the idea waits.
Name the cost of a change of direction
Before you change direction, write the one constraint it breaks (budget, team or time) and who will carry it. Then hand over the first three steps, not only the vision.
games: The idea only counts when someone else can act on it, under a timer.
Every move is a change under a constraint; over-adjusting brings it down.
VO.exercise: Before your next change of direction, write the one constraint it breaks and hand over the first three steps.
best: Creating a brand or a category
avoid: Changing direction without naming what it costs
Handing over a vision without the first three steps
Operating work that needs the same thing done well every day
VO.ladder: From here, The Ultimate Alchemist is reached by adding the other two Alchemist ways of executing to your own. From the Magnetic Perfectionist: a quality bar the story has to meet before it ships. From the Energetic Empath: the people carried with you, with clear commitments. The Ultimate Alchemist holds all three: the vision, the quality and the people, with proof.

SB.is: A Systemised Builder is an Architect who executes by making things run. Once a decision is made, you turn it into a routine: the procedure, the checks and the people who own each step, so it happens the same way every time without you. You win by reliability: output that can be counted on.
exec: When time is cut
You protect the flow: the routine and the system that keep things running. A plan or a feature can wait; the thing that runs every day cannot.
Your rhythm
You work continuously. A weekly routine keeps everything moving, with daily checks when something is new or fragile.
Keeping scope in bounds
You standardise. Once something works, it becomes the way it is done, and what is not in the standard is not done.
The first thing you create
A checklist or a step-by-step procedure. Before a roadmap or a dashboard, you want the steps written down.
Under pressure
You add process: more structure, more routine. When something breaks, you put daily checks on it until it runs smoothly again, then write a procedure so it does not happen again.
wrong: Invents too little
The routine runs well and nothing new is tried, because new things do not have a procedure yet.
Process where it is not needed
A one-off gets a checklist. The overhead of the system costs more than the thing it controls.
Resists change
A better way is turned down because the current way works. Playbooks go out of date while they are still followed.
Improving one area at the expense of the whole
The part you own runs perfectly and the business around it is starved, because the measure was the part, not the whole.
improve: Protect capacity for experiments
Keep 10 to 15% of capacity for things that have no procedure yet, and let them fail without a post-mortem.
Change control with a log
Record each problem and its fix, and review the log monthly so the playbook changes with the business.
Measure the whole
Add one measure that belongs to the business, not to your area, to every weekly review.
games: The routine has to keep running while what arrives keeps changing.
You play the tiles you are dealt, not the word you planned: a small experiment every turn.
The rules of the round change with every card; a fixed routine loses.
SB.exercise: Block 10% of next week for something that has no procedure yet.
best: Scaling once the product sells reliably
avoid: Putting a procedure on something you have done once
Keeping a playbook that the business has outgrown
Starting from nothing, where there is nothing yet to systemise
SB.ladder: From here, The Ultimate Architect is reached by adding the other two Architect ways of executing to your own. From the Master Strategist: an order of moves, so the system serves a direction. From the Internal Analyser: a test before a change becomes the standard. The Ultimate Architect holds all three: the sequence, the proof and the system.

EE.is: An Energetic Empath is an Alchemist who executes through people. Once a decision is made, you turn it into a cause: who is involved, why they care, the shared win, and the next step each person takes. You win by momentum: people move because you moved them.
exec: When time is cut
You protect the people: the momentum and the relationships around the work. The plan, the standard and the story bend before the team does.
Your rhythm
You work in conversations. You talk with the people involved until you are aligned, then move together, in short bursts with clear goals.
Keeping scope in bounds
You agree the scope with the people involved and hold everyone to it. Scope is a commitment, not a list.
The first thing you create
A list of the people involved and what each has committed to. Before a roadmap or a brief, you want to know who is in.
Under pressure
You rally the people around it. When something breaks, you get everyone together, clear the tension and agree the way through.
wrong: Boundaries slip
Every ask is a yes, because saying no costs a relationship. Your capacity goes before your commitments do.
Focus spreads
Many partners, many causes, and no one thing finished. Energy is spent where people are, not where the business needs it.
Waits for everyone to agree
A decision that needed one person waits for the room. Alignment becomes the goal instead of the result.
Soft commitments and unclear ownership
Everyone is in and no one owns it. Wins are celebrated and not written down, so they cannot be repeated.
improve: An exit rule for every partnership
Before a partnership or pilot starts, write its time limit and the condition that ends it. Review it on that date, not when it starts to feel wrong.
Wins written down within a week
After each win, write who did what and what it produced. A win that is written down can be repeated without you in the room.
One owner and one decider per task
For each piece of work, name the one person responsible and the one who decides. Alignment is for the direction; it is not needed for every step.
games: Every deal has a price and saying no is a move; bankruptcy is a hard exit rule.
Folding is saying no; one decision at a time, on your own read.
EE.exercise: Write the exit rule for one current partnership and the single owner for one shared task.
avoid: A commitment made in the room that the capacity cannot carry
A partnership with no exit rule
Deep solo analysis that needs no one else
EE.ladder: From here, The Ultimate Alchemist is reached by adding the other two Alchemist ways of executing to your own. From the Visionary Oracle: a direction the people are moving towards. From the Magnetic Perfectionist: a quality bar the shared work has to meet. The Ultimate Alchemist holds all three: the vision, the quality and the people, with proof.

MP.is: A Magnetic Perfectionist is an Alchemist who executes by making the thing right. Once a decision is made, you turn it into a standard: what it has to look and feel like, the details that matter, and the quality bar it must meet. You win by pull: people want what you made because of how it is made.
exec: When time is cut
You protect the quality: what it looks and feels like, and the details that matter. Scope and speed give way before the standard does.
Your rhythm
You work in polish cycles. Refine until it is right, with a date to put it out. The date is the only thing that stops the polishing.
Keeping scope in bounds
You set the quality bar and cut everything that falls below it. Scope is controlled by standard, not by list.
The first thing you create
A quality bar: the standard the result must meet. Before a roadmap or a story, you define what good looks like.
Under pressure
You hold the quality bar, or raise it. When something breaks, you refine the part that failed until it is right, with a date to put it back out.
wrong: Hesitates to ship
The date moves because the work is not yet right. Customers wait for a version they would have paid for last month.
Scope grows
Each refinement reveals another detail that matters. The standard rises and the ship date goes with it.
Overspends
Quality is bought at a cost the business limits cannot carry.
Polishing what customers do not value
The detail you refined is one the customer never noticed, while the one they asked for waits.
improve: One ship day a week
Pick one day a week on which something goes out, whatever state it is in. Sort the work into red (must be right), amber (should be) and green (can wait). Only red stops the ship.
The quality bar written next to the limits
Write the quality bar with the budget and the date beside it. If all three cannot be met, the standard is lowered in the open, not the date moved in silence.
Polish only what the customer noticed
Each month look at activation, retention and willingness to pay. Keep refining the detail that moved one of them; stop refining the detail that moved none.
games: A rough drawing that is understood beats a perfect one that is not finished.
You lose by waiting: accuse before you are certain, or another player will.
MP.exercise: Set a 20-minute timer on one piece of work you would normally polish for an hour, and send what exists when it rings.
avoid: A launch where speed matters more than finish
Refining without a ship date
Spending on quality the margin cannot carry
MP.ladder: From here, The Ultimate Alchemist is reached by adding the other two Alchemist ways of executing to your own. From the Visionary Oracle: a direction the quality serves, so the standard points somewhere. From the Energetic Empath: the people carried with you, with clear commitments. The Ultimate Alchemist holds all three: the vision, the quality and the people, with proof.

UA.is: The Ultimate Architect is an Architect who holds all three Architect ways of executing at once. Once a decision is made, you set the order of moves, prove each one with a test, and turn what works into a system that runs without you. You win by integration: strategy, proof and systems that reinforce each other.
exec: When time is cut
You protect all three at once: the plan, the system and the data, adjusted together rather than one sacrificed for another.
Your rhythm
Moves set in blocks, a weekly routine to run them, and tests to prove them. Strategy sprints alternate with operations sprints.
Keeping scope in bounds
The chosen moves set the scope, standards hold it, and analysis gates what is added.
The first thing you create
A one-page map that links the roadmap, the procedures and the tests, so all three can be seen together.
Under pressure
You re-plan, tighten the process and check the data at once. When something breaks, you re-align the plan, the process and the data behind it together.
wrong: Overload from switching
Strategy, systems and proof all need you, and switching between them costs more than any one of them.
An empire for its own sake
The structure grows because it can, not because a customer asked for it.
A weak story for customers
Everything inside the business is right and the outside world cannot say what you do.
improve: Working prototypes
Keep testing ideas with a working version, not a plan for one. The prototype is the proof.
Outside challenge to the story
Invite someone outside the business to challenge the customer story every quarter.
One review, two measures
A monthly strategy and operations review with two measures only: impact and stability.
UA.gamesIntro: Do you find you excel at the following games? Keep playing them and improve your scores or levels to help you stay at this level.
UA.exercise: Invite one outsider to challenge your customer story this month.
avoid: Growing the structure faster than the customer story
Carrying all three roles yourself as the team grows
UA.ladder: You are at the top of the Architect ladder. Staying there means keeping the three ways of executing in balance: the Master Strategist’s sequence, the Internal Analyser’s proof and the Systemised Builder’s system. When one of the three goes quiet, the others start to fail with it.

UAl.is: The Ultimate Alchemist is an Alchemist who holds all three Alchemist ways of executing at once. Once a decision is made, you set the direction, hold the quality bar and carry the people with you, and you prove it with results. You win by integration: a story that converts, a product that pulls and a community that scales, with proof.
exec: When time is cut
You protect all three at once: the vision, the quality and the people, kept in step rather than one sacrificed for another.
Your rhythm
Show it, refine it and bring people with it, in step. Bursts of demos followed by consolidation.
Keeping scope in bounds
Explore, then set the bar, with everyone agreed on what is in and what is out.
The first thing you create
A one-page vision that links the story, the standard and the people.
Under pressure
You re-tell the story, hold the quality and rally the people at once. When something breaks, you re-harmonise the idea, the quality and the people together.
wrong: Promising more than the systems can deliver
The story and the product pull people in faster than operations can serve them.
The story outgrows operations
Each demo raises expectations; the consolidation that should follow is skipped for the next demo.

Visual: You take information in best when you can see it: a diagram, a chart, a sketch of how the parts fit. A page of text slows you; the same content as a picture lands at once.
Ask for the diagram first and the explanation second.
Auditory: You take information in best when you hear it: a conversation, a talk, something repeated aloud. You learn by asking questions and hearing the answer.
Talk it through, and keep a recording of any explanation you will need again.
Read/Write: You take information in best when you can read it and write it down: text, lists, notes. Writing it out is how you think it through.
Ask for it in writing, and make your own notes before you act on it.
Kinaesthetic: You take information in best by doing: open the tool, enter your own numbers, try it until it makes sense. A demonstration helps less than a go.
Ask for a template you can change, not a description of one.
Multimodal: No single way leads. You use whichever format fits the task, which makes you flexible and means you sometimes have to choose.
Pick the format by the job: a diagram for a structure, a conversation for a judgement, a template for a method.
Structured: You learn step by step, in order, each piece built on the last. Skipping ahead costs you; a long guide read from the first page works.
Ask for the order of the steps before the detail.
Global: You need the whole first, then the detail. Until you can see how it fits together, no single part makes sense.
Ask for the overview or the map first; skim before you read.
Adaptive: You move between the two: an overview for new ground, step by step once you are in it, and you work well alone or with others.
Decide at the start which the task needs, then switch deliberately.
Concrete: An idea makes sense to you through facts, details and a real example from a business like yours. A principle on its own does not land until you see it applied.
Ask for the worked case, with numbers.
Abstract: An idea makes sense to you through the principle: why it works and where else it applies. Once you have the pattern, the examples follow.
Ask for the rule first, then one example.
Flexible: You move between the two: the example when an idea is new, the principle to carry it somewhere else.
Ask for both, and notice which one you reach for when it is new.
Individual: You learn something difficult best alone, at your own rhythm. Discussion before you have thought it through costs you focus.
Prepare alone before any group session, and say so.
Collaborative: You learn something difficult best with other people: discussion and shared energy. Talking it through is how it becomes clear.
Find a partner, a group or a course with others for anything hard.
Fast: You learn in short, intense bursts; momentum carries you. A long, slow module loses you.
Ask for the key deliverables and sprint through them; add the depth afterwards.
Slow: You learn steadily and methodically; depth over speed. Under time pressure you ask for a longer timeline to keep accuracy.
Protect the time. Do not trade accuracy for a deadline that can be moved.
Versatile: You learn fast when you need to and slowly for mastery.
Decide which the task is before you start, and do not let urgency decide for you.

Low-risk learning paths, gradual wins and predictable milestones.

Can overlook other views or warning signs

A prompt to look for evidence against the decision before committing.

Delays or reverses decisions; gives authority to others

Small, safe decisions to build a record, and mentor check-ins after each decision.

The same short check before each decision.

Milestone approvals, structured tests and checkpoints before scaling.

Run one experiment that is safe to fail each month, and increase exposure gradually.
Safety buffers, experiments that are safe to fail, a gradual increase in exposure.
Outward: You are energised by people, collaboration and momentum.
Builds momentum through people and collaboration
Too much time with others; scattered focus
Protect solo follow-through time after every live session.
Live sessions balanced with solo follow-through.
Inward: You are energised by time alone and deep thinking.
Share one written idea a week, and send a brief before every meeting.
Written channels, protected deep-work time, briefs before meetings.

Quick launches, with a check before each stage of scaling.

A ready-to-ship standard agreed in advance.

Give every experiment a review point, and keep only what works.
Experiments with review points to keep what works.

Improvement cycles, with set windows to test new ideas.

Put one customer story next to every figure you report.
Reports in figures, with customer stories alongside.

Put two figures under every story you tell.
Reports in customer stories, with a short summary of the figures.
Collaborators: You see others in your market as people to work with.
Agree roles and boundaries before any partnership starts.
Partnerships with agreed roles and boundaries.

Benchmarks against others in the market.

Plans include resource and feasibility checks.

Run small tests that make more of what you already have.
Plans include small tests that make more of existing resources.
Both: You hold both beliefs; which one leads depends on the situation. This is not a lack of view.

Shows both framings, and uses the one that fits the situation you described.

A spending limit for each stage.
Purpose + Stories: The impact is clear to you but harder to show to investors.
Each story paired with two figures.
Craft + Competitors: You want it right and you want to be ahead.
A ship date and a quality standard agreed together.
New + Limited: Many new ideas with tight resources.
A limit on how many new ideas run at once.
